The Hub is what opens when you sign in. It's a short read, not a dashboard
you have to study — your venue at the top, a couple of numbers, and the one
list worth acting on.

Direct URL: `rumizi.com/your-venue/w/hub`.

## Your venue, up top

Your logo (or hero image, if you haven't set a logo) and venue name sit at
the top of the page. If that space looks empty, you haven't uploaded
either — see [Brand images](/vendors/venue/brand).

## The 7-day snapshot

Two cards, each showing the last seven days with the week-over-week change
underneath. When there isn't enough history to compare, you'll see **"Not
enough data yet"** rather than a misleading percentage.

<Columns cols={2}>
  <Card title="Questions answered by AI" icon="message-circle">
    How many times the menu assistant answered a diner at your venue.
    This is the honest measure of whether the chat is earning its keep.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Menu views" icon="eye">
    How many times your menu was opened, with today's count underneath.
  </Card>
</Columns>

<Note>
**Menu views currently reads 0.** The per-day counting behind it isn't
wired up yet, so treat the card as a placeholder until it starts moving.
The AI answers card is live and accurate.
</Note>

## Least loved dishes

Diners can mark a dish **Not for me** while browsing (see
[Scan and browse](/diners/scan-and-browse#not-for-me)). The Hub collects
those marks and shows the dishes with the most, along with the reasons
diners picked — *"too expensive"*, *"don't like the ingredients"*, and so
on — or **"No reasons given"** when they skipped that step.

This is the closest thing Rumizi gives you to the feedback a diner would
never say to your face.

<Warning>
Small counts are noisy. Three marks on a dish is a hint, not a verdict —
it might be one table having an off night. Wait for a pattern before you
change a recipe or pull a dish.
</Warning>

The card only appears when there's something in it. No marks, no card.
It's fully anonymous — you see what was marked and why, never who marked
it.

<Tip>
A dish collecting marks isn't always a bad dish. Check the reasons first:
"too expensive" is a pricing decision, "not what I expected" is usually a
description or photo problem, and both are cheaper to fix than the recipe.
</Tip>
